# A runtime generated by Mica

Status: draft for discussion. No implementation is part of this proposal.
Date: 2026-09-26.
Revised: 2026-09-27.
Code baseline: local `main` at `74193f5`.

## 1. Proposal

Write a Mica library that constructs native programs as relations and emits C.
Use that library to describe and generate the Omica VM and runtime.
Run the generator on the existing Odin runtime first, then on the generated runtime.

The Mica compiler continues to compile ordinary Mica into bytecode.
The generated VM runs that compiler, the generator, and ordinary applications.
The external C compiler translates the generated runtime into machine code.

```text
Mica runtime descriptions + Mica generation library
                       |
           run on existing Odin Omica
                       |
              program facts + rules
                       |
            checked, ordered native IR
                       |
                  generated C
                       |
            C compiler + platform shim
                       |
                 native Omica
                       |
       runs the same Mica generator again
```

The relational representation is the central design choice.
It lets ordinary Mica queries connect runtime definitions, generated code, analyses, diagnostics, and coverage checks.
For example, one opcode definition can supply its encoding, operand checks, dispatch entry, and disassembler metadata.

The agreed direction is self-bootstrapping through C generation, with runtime conversion as the goal.
The schemas, module names, platform boundary, and migration stages below are proposals.

## 2. Terms and proposed source layout

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Generator | Mica code that constructs, checks, lowers, and emits a native program |
| Runtime description | Mica code and facts that define the VM, kernel, and runtime algorithms |
| Native IR | Typed program facts with explicit control flow, order, and memory operations |
| Generated runtime | The native executable produced from generated C |
| Platform shim | A small native library for OS services and target-specific primitives |
| Closed bootstrap | A generated runtime can regenerate and rebuild itself without Odin |
| Runtime parity | The replacement meets the declared compatibility and behavior contract |

Proposed directories:

| Path | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `apps/native/` | Reusable builders, schemas, analyses, diagnostics, and C emission |
| `apps/runtime/` | Runtime descriptions, opcode definitions, and value definitions |
| `native/platform/` | Reviewed C shim and platform headers |
| `tools/native-bootstrap/` | Stage orchestration, manifests, and comparison commands |
| `build/native/` | Generated files and build artifacts, excluded from source control |

These paths do not exist as part of this proposal.
The reusable library must generate small standalone C programs without importing the runtime descriptions.

## 3. Existing foundations and remaining work

The [Mica parser](../apps/compiler/parse.mica) already constructs a relational AST with columns `node`, `role`, `target`, and `ordinal`.
Its `parse_rows` entry point also exposes the facts as a list.
The [Mica emitter](../apps/compiler/emit.mica) consumes those rows and constructs a bytecode program.
This is a precedent for relational program data, rather than an existing native backend.

The compiler still calls the Odin [`assemble` builtin](../mica/runtime/builtins.odin).
The [program artifact codec](../mica/vm/program_bytes.odin) also lives in Odin.
A closed bootstrap must replace those dependencies, together with the world initialization path and required builtins.

The [bootstrap tool](../tools/bootstrap/main.odin) and [self-differential tool](../tools/selfdiff/main.odin) provide useful compiler checks.
They do not establish a native runtime bootstrap.
The new harness must compare successive native generations and run without Odin after the initial seed.

The runtime migration covers several coupled components:

| Current source | Required behavior |
| --- | --- |
| [`mica/var`](../mica/var) | Tagged values, heap objects, equality, ordering, hashing, and allocation ownership |
| [`mica/vm`](../mica/vm) | Bytecode, artifact loading, frames, dispatch, errors, and suspension requests |
| [`mica/kernel`](../mica/kernel) | Relations, queries, rules, transactions, authority, snapshots, and reclamation |
| [`mica/runtime`](../mica/runtime) | Builtins, world initialization, tasks, scheduling, mailboxes, and subscriptions |
| [`mica/buffer`](../mica/buffer) | Buffer storage and operations |
| [`mica/store`](../mica/store) | Value encoding, durable commits, recovery, and checkpoints |

Hosts and external integrations need an explicit compatibility inventory.
They can follow the first closed bootstrap, but their absence prevents a claim of complete replacement.

## 4. Scope and completion criteria

The immediate objective is the bounded construction experiment in section 13.
Its review determines whether the authoring model is suitable for runtime conversion.
The later objectives are a closed bootstrap for a declared runtime profile, then parity with the selected Odin baseline.
Neither bootstrap closure nor the experiment establishes support for all existing host applications.

The replacement contract targets Omica at the selected Odin revision.
The shared Mica language contract remains the basis for decisions about behavioural differences.
Rust can supply independent comparisons and potentially run the generator.
Its assembly interface, ownership implementation, and host services are separate contracts.
This proposal does not require replacement of the Rust runtime or compatibility with its bytecode artifacts.

### 4.1 Bootstrap profile

The proposed profile uses one worker, memory storage, and a fresh world for each build.
Before runtime conversion starts, its inventory must name each required operation, dependency, and independent acceptance case.
The inventory includes dependencies of the compiler, generator, runtime descriptions, and their initialization code.
The inventory includes dependencies reached through indirect calls and registered callbacks.

| Area | Required inventory |
| --- | --- |
| Values and execution | Value kinds, collection operations, calls, closures, errors, and bytecode instructions used by the build |
| Compiler services | Source loading, assembly, artifact codecs, installation, and catalogue initialization |
| Relations and analyses | Schemas, indexes, queries, joins, recursive rules, stratified negation, and pass boundaries used by the generator |
| Transactions and lifetime | Commit, abort, retained snapshots, arena ownership, and any required suspension boundaries |
| Build host | Source input, generated output, diagnostics, and the protocol used by the external build harness |

Durability, parallel scheduling, interactive hosts, and unrelated applications remain outside this profile unless the inventory identifies a dependency.
Unsupported operations fail explicitly. They cannot silently succeed or use an undeclared native fallback.
The inventory must account for kernel dependencies before stage D begins.
One worker narrows scheduling work but does not remove the relational engine needed by the generator.

### 4.2 Closed bootstrap

A closed bootstrap requires all of the following:

1. The generated runtime runs the Mica compiler and generator.
2. It compiles their source and regenerates its own C output.
3. An external C toolchain builds the next runtime from that output.
4. Successive generations produce identical generated sources and manifests for identical inputs.
5. Each generated runtime passes the bootstrap conformance suite.
6. The process needs no Odin executable, library, compiler, or hidden service after the seed stage.

The allowed external dependencies are the C toolchain, OS libraries, and declared platform shim.
Release artifacts can include generated C so a fresh machine can build the seed without an installed Mica runtime.
Published artifacts must identify the source revision and generation manifest.

The builder API is an embedded systems language expressed through ordinary Mica calls and facts.
It needs defined types, memory operations, control flow, calling conventions, ownership contracts, and diagnostics.
It adds no systems syntax to Mica and does not convert the existing Mica compiler to native code.
Readable descriptions of actual runtime algorithms are an acceptance criterion for the first experiment.
JIT compilation, removal of the external toolchain, and simultaneous native backends are outside the initial scope.

## 5. Program construction

### 5.1 Verbs construct programs, rules describe properties

Ordinary Mica verbs provide builders for records, functions, blocks, instructions, and declarations.
Each builder returns an explicit node identifier and the updated construction state.
Builders collect facts in batches before publishing them for analysis.

Rules derive properties over those facts.
Examples include function reachability, propagated effects, missing implementations, and incompatible field uses.
Ordinary verbs perform constructive lowering and emit text in a defined order.

Rule evaluation must not allocate fresh node identifiers.
Recursive analyses operate on a finite domain, and negation must remain stratified.
This restriction keeps analysis termination separate from code construction.

The native program does not inherit the runtime behavior of its builder verbs.
A Mica loop in the generator constructs repeated program fragments during generation.
A loop node in the native IR produces a loop that runs inside the generated runtime.
The API must make this distinction visible.

### 5.2 Build scope and fact ownership

The initial generator uses a dedicated, disposable world for each build.
Each analysis pass reads a frozen input snapshot and writes a separate result relation family.
Lowering creates a new representation with provenance links to its input.
No pass silently changes the facts that another pass analyzes.

The build records its source digest, schema version, target, feature profile, and generation settings.
Multiple builds in one world are deferred.
That later design requires an explicit build key on every relation and rule.

The current kernel supports batch ingestion and suspended derivation.
The generator uses explicit construction and analysis boundaries to avoid full derivation after every builder operation.
This design does not depend on incremental maintenance from pending changes.

### 5.3 Relations and keys

Use specific relations for core structures.
The following schema is illustrative notation, not executable Mica:

```text
Function(function, symbol, result_type)
Parameter(function, position, variable, type)
Record(record, symbol)
Field(record, position, symbol, type)
Local(function, variable, type)
Block(block, function)
EntryBlock(function, block)
Instruction(block, position, instruction)
Operation(instruction, opcode)
Operand(instruction, position, value)
Result(instruction, variable)
Terminator(block, instruction)
BranchTarget(instruction, position, block)
Constant(value, type, encoding)
Origin(node, source, line, column)
LoweredFrom(output_node, input_node)
```

The schema declares functional keys and reference constraints explicitly.
For example, `(function, position)` identifies one parameter, and `(block, position)` identifies one instruction.
The checker rejects conflicting rows instead of selecting an arbitrary match.
Each block has exactly one terminator, outside its ordinary instruction sequence.

Relations are sets, so neither insertion order nor iteration order defines execution order.
Positions define parameter, field, argument, and instruction order.
Branch target positions distinguish the true and false destinations.
Repeated effects retain distinct instruction identities, even with identical operands.

Node identifiers are local handles, not persistent symbol names.
Emission uses stable logical names and deterministic traversal.
Symbol interning order, world identities, and hash iteration must not affect output.

### 5.4 Types, values, and control flow

The initial native types include fixed-width integers, `f32`, booleans, pointers, arrays, records, and function signatures.
Semantic types such as `Value`, `RegisterIndex`, and `RelationId` remain distinct despite equal physical representations.
Explicit operations convert between semantic and physical types.

Structured builders expose conditionals, loops, calls, and local variables.
Lowering produces basic blocks with ordered instructions and explicit terminators.
The first implementation uses typed mutable locals rather than SSA and phi nodes.
The C compiler performs native optimization.

Operands in the lowered IR are constants or variable references.
Calls, loads, stores, and other ordered operations occupy separate instructions.
Lowering places effectful argument expressions into ordered temporaries before a C call.
Short-circuit boolean expressions lower to branches.
These rules prevent C evaluation order from changing Mica runtime behavior.

Definite-assignment analysis checks every path before a local read.
Type checks cover calls, fields, return values, and conversions.
Control-flow checks reject invalid targets, missing terminators, and paths without required returns.
Initial checks can use ordinary verbs where relational rules make the implementation less clear.

## 6. What the relational model buys us

### 6.1 One opcode definition, several consistent artifacts

The runtime description contains opcode facts and handler bodies:

```text
Opcode(opcode, encoding, name)
OpcodeOperand(opcode, position, role, representation)
Implementation(opcode, function)
OpcodeEffect(opcode, effect)
BoundaryRequest(opcode, request_kind)
```

These facts supply the opcode enum, operand checker, dispatch cases, disassembler metadata, and coverage manifest.
Handler bodies still express the actual algorithms through native builders.
Metadata does not synthesize the semantics of an opcode.

For an arithmetic opcode, its handler reads registers, calls a checked value operation, and branches to the runtime error path on failure.
The builder constructs those operations once.
Queries can then connect the handler to allocation effects, called helpers, and its generated C location.

The checker rejects duplicate encodings and missing handlers.
Independent behavior tests still supply expected arithmetic results and errors.
Tests generated from the same opcode facts cannot establish that those facts are correct.

### 6.2 Value coverage

```text
ValueKind(kind, tag)
ImmediateKind(kind)
HeapKind(kind, record)
ValueOperation(kind, operation, implementation)
PersistencePolicy(kind, policy)
```

Queries expose missing equality, hashing, ordering, copy, display, and serialization behavior for each value kind.
Persistence policy explicitly identifies kinds that cannot enter durable storage.
The generator rejects omissions rather than inventing default behavior.

The facts also connect record layouts to allocation and traversal helpers.
They do not prove that a pointer remains valid or that reclamation is safe.
Those properties need explicit ownership rules and runtime tests.

### 6.3 Transitive analyses

The following rules use schematic Datalog notation:

```text
Needed(f)          :- EntryPoint(f).
Needed(g)          :- Needed(f), Calls(f, g).
MayAllocate(f)     :- AllocatesDirectly(f).
MayAllocate(f)     :- Calls(f, g), MayAllocate(g).
AllocationError(f) :- MustNotAllocate(f), MayAllocate(f).
```

The same pattern can propagate blocking, suspension, transaction requirements, and authority effects.
A diagnostic includes the call path that caused the violation.
That path connects derived facts back to runtime description locations.

The checker derives `Calls` from call instructions in the checked IR.
It derives direct effects from memory operations, boundary operations, and foreign declarations.
Ordinary function summaries follow their bodies. Authors do not maintain a separate call graph or assert that an unchecked body is pure.
Each lowering pass must preserve these effects, and the checker repeats the analysis on the final IR before C emission.

Foreign calls require declared effects and ownership contracts.
Those declarations are trusted inputs that require review against the foreign implementation.
Indirect calls require a conservative target set or an unknown-effect marker.
Unknown effects cannot satisfy a no-allocation or no-blocking contract.
Reachability roots include exported functions and registered callbacks.
Code removal remains disabled until the root model covers all indirect entry paths.

### 6.4 Queryable diagnostics

Diagnostics are facts with a code, severity, node, and explanation.
Additional relations record the evidence behind each diagnostic.
The command-line renderer and development tools read the same result.

Useful queries include:

- Which builtin handlers can suspend while they hold a transaction?
- Which value kinds lack a persistence policy?
- Which dispatch cases reach an allocation helper?
- Which generated instructions came from this runtime description?
- Which foreign functions remain in the bootstrap dependency graph?

These are generation-time queries.
The native VM runs ordinary compiled code and does not query its own instruction facts during dispatch.

## 7. A small construction example

The first standalone example generates a function that extracts the value tag.
This is API pseudocode, not a promise about Mica syntax or final builder names:

```text
fn = function("mica_value_tag", result = U8)
word = parameter(fn, "word", U64)
entry = block(fn)
shifted = instruction(entry, LogicalShiftRight, word, constant(U64, "56"))
tag = instruction(entry, Truncate, shifted, U8)
return_value(entry, tag)
```

Builders construct function, parameter, instruction, operand, and type facts.
Analysis checks the operands and return type.
The emitter produces ordinary C:

```c
uint8_t mica_value_tag(uint64_t word) {
    uint64_t shifted = word >> 56;
    uint8_t tag = (uint8_t)shifted;
    return tag;
}
```

The generator represents wide integer literals as checked text, bytes, or limbs.
Mica integers cannot hold every `uint64_t` bit pattern.
The initial proposal uses canonical hexadecimal text with explicit type and range checks.
This matters for tag masks and encoded values, beyond this small example.

## 8. C emission and native contracts

C is the first backend because it provides a direct route from explicit native operations to ordinary executables.
The initial target is C11 on a declared 64-bit platform profile.
The generator emits headers, translation units, a symbol map, and a build manifest.
It emits function prototypes before uses and orders record definitions by layout dependencies.

The checked native IR is separate from C declarations and textual formatting.
This separation leaves room for another backend without requiring a general backend framework now.
No portability claim extends beyond the tested target profiles.

The current [value ABI](../mica/var/value.odin) uses a 64-bit word, an 8-bit tag, and a 56-bit payload.
Integers are signed 56-bit values.
Floats use finite `f32` values with canonicalized negative zero.
The first replacement preserves these semantics and the declared value ABI.

Native operations must define behavior at the C boundary:

- Checked arithmetic preserves Mica integer limits and error behavior.
- Bit operations use unsigned representations and checked shift counts.
- Bit reinterpretation uses defined mechanisms such as `memcpy`.
- Float conversion preserves finite-value and zero rules.
- Pointer packing checks the supported address range and target ABI.
- Record access respects alignment and aliasing requirements.
- Atomic operations carry explicit memory-order requirements.

These are contracts for the native library and emitter, not consequences of using relations.
The target profile and generated assertions reject unsupported representations.
Compatibility also requires explicit byte order and version checks in artifact and storage codecs.

The initial emitter has no arbitrary C expression or statement escape.
Foreign declarations name typed functions with effects and ownership contracts.
Exceptional native code lives in reviewed shim files that the manifest lists.
This boundary prevents opaque strings from becoming the runtime implementation.

## 9. Runtime ownership and platform boundary

The runtime descriptions own value semantics, VM dispatch, relational evaluation, transactions, scheduling policy, and persistence formats.
The platform shim owns OS calls and target-specific primitives.

| Generated runtime | Platform shim |
| --- | --- |
| Arena policy, snapshot ownership, reclamation protocol | Memory allocation and mapping primitives |
| Task queues, mailbox semantics, suspension policy | Threads, mutexes, condition variables, clocks |
| WAL records, commit ordering, recovery decisions | File access, synchronization, rename, directory operations |
| Host request protocol and authority checks | Transport adapters and process integration |

The shim cannot hide a second VM, rule evaluator, or transaction implementation.
Its public interface must remain small enough to inspect as part of the bootstrap dependency manifest.
C library dependencies also appear in that manifest.

The first port preserves the existing ownership model.
Heap values remain immutable, with snapshot and transaction arenas responsible for their lifetime.
The migration must account for existing specialized ownership optimizations.
It does not introduce a garbage collector or redesign concurrent reclamation at the same time.

Each pointer parameter and result declares its owner, borrowing lifetime, and any ownership transfer.
Allocation operations define failure results and the cleanup required on each exit path.
Arena release remains the lifetime boundary for arena-owned values.

The initial checker requires these declarations and checks types and explicit transfers against function contracts.
It does not prove arbitrary pointer lifetimes, bounds, aliasing, or concurrent reclamation.
Those remain obligations of the runtime descriptions and foreign implementations, with independent tests and sanitizer checks.
The first experiment must expose these limits in its string construction and arena release paths.

VM boundaries must preserve observable task behavior.
The current [task implementation](../mica/runtime/task.odin) commits or aborts staged effects and renews transactions across suspension.
The replacement must preserve those boundaries, authority checks, error handling, and resumption behavior.
Generating a dispatch loop alone does not preserve this contract.

## 10. Closing the bootstrap

Let `R0` be the existing Odin runtime and `G` the generator plus runtime descriptions.
Let `C1` be the first generated C artifact set and `R1` its compiled runtime.
The sequence is:

```text
R0 compiles and runs G  -> C1 -> C toolchain -> R1
R1 compiles and runs G  -> C2 -> C toolchain -> R2
R2 compiles and runs G  -> C3 -> C toolchain -> R3

Required: C1 == C2 == C3, plus conformance for R1, R2, and R3.
```

Each generated stage must also compile the Mica compiler sources.
A seed compiler artifact can start that process, but each stage must replace it with a compiler artifact built on that stage.
The harness then uses that rebuilt compiler to compile `G`.
This prevents a permanently embedded seed compiler from concealing an incomplete loop.

Equality covers generated source, headers, stable metadata, and manifests.
Manifests exclude timestamps, absolute workspace paths, and temporary identifiers.
Native binary equality is a separate reproducible-build check because toolchains can add variable metadata.
Source equality alone does not establish semantic correctness.

The generator dependency inventory must include:

- Values, collections, symbols, errors, and ordinary bytecode execution.
- Compiler support, assembly, artifact loading, and world initialization.
- Relations, queries, rules, and the transaction operations used by generation.
- File output and the host protocol required by the build harness.

The generator uses the relational engine to generate its successor.
There is no foundational cycle during the first build because `R0` supplies that engine.
There is a substantial migration requirement before `R1` can replace `R0`.
An arithmetic-only VM demonstration is useful, but cannot close this bootstrap.

## 11. Migration stages

Each stage has an observable result and a completion gate.
The stages express dependency order, not an effort estimate.

| Stage | Deliverable | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A: construction library | Typed builders, relations, checks, and C emission | The section 13 experiment passes correctness, ownership, determinism, and readability review |
| B: value layer | Generated tags, layouts, value operations, and coverage checks | Independent cases match Odin values, limits, errors, and encodings |
| C: VM | Generated bytecode loader, frames, handlers, dispatch, and boundary protocol | VM conformance and differential execution pass for the declared subset |
| D: bootstrap profile | Kernel, builtins, compiler services, and build host from the section 4.1 inventory | Every inventory case passes and the generated runtime compiles and runs the complete generator |
| E: closed bootstrap | Stage harness, dependency manifest, and repeat generation | Three generations agree, pass conformance, and require no Odin after the seed |
| F: runtime parity | Remaining scheduler, storage, buffers, and host integration | The declared compatibility matrix passes, including concurrency and recovery |

Intermediate builds can link temporary native helpers.
Each helper must appear in the manifest with its intended replacement.
Stage E permits only the declared platform shim and external libraries.
Odin adapters and handwritten runtime algorithms cannot survive that gate under a shim label.

The section 4.1 profile bounds stages D and E.
Any additional dependency requires an explicit profile change and an acceptance case.
Stage F restores the selected concurrency, durability, and host contract before replacement claims extend to those features.

## 12. Validation and cost controls

Construction checks run before C emission.
The test suite includes malformed facts, conflicting keys, undefined locals, incorrect call types, and invalid control flow.
Determinism tests permute fact insertion order and symbol creation order.
Expected output remains identical.

Native tests compare values, errors, observable effects, and artifact behavior against independent fixtures and the Odin implementation.
The suite includes integer limits, invalid shifts, aliasing-sensitive accesses, and float edge cases.
Sanitizer builds exercise allocation, lifetime, and concurrency paths.
Persistence tests include abort, recovery, and interrupted commit cases.

The bootstrap harness records all executable and library dependencies.
Its post-seed environment excludes Odin tools and artifacts.
A successful build in that environment checks that the loop has no accidental Odin dependency.

Generated tests complement independent tests.
Coverage derived from runtime facts catches omissions, but cannot detect every shared specification error.
The Odin implementation is a comparison target, not an infallible definition of behavior.
Disagreements require examination against the language contract.

Generation cost also matters.
Each stage records fact counts, derivation rounds, elapsed time, peak memory, generated source size, and C compilation time.
The first performance gate is completion of the real generator workload within a declared budget.
Runtime parity also needs representative application workloads.
This proposal makes no speed claim from C generation alone.

Development output stays in ignored build directories or temporary storage.
This includes generated C, intermediate facts, manifests, timing samples, logs, and test reports.
Source control contains maintained generator and runtime sources, build commands, and focused regression cases.
Release C archives and their provenance are published artifacts, separate from development output.

## 13. Decisions to argue about

These are initial positions, not settled requirements.

| Decision | Proposed default | Alternative and consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Authoring interface | Structured builders over typed program facts | Direct relation authoring is concise for metadata but cumbersome for ordered algorithms |
| IR form | Basic blocks, ordered instructions, typed mutable locals | SSA adds analysis structure and construction complexity before bootstrap needs it |
| Relation schema | Specific relations with explicit keys | A universal edge relation simplifies extension but moves more errors into late checks |
| Analysis boundary | Batch construction followed by frozen snapshots | Continuous derivation supports live feedback but adds cost and invalidation complexity |
| Build isolation | One disposable world per build | Shared worlds enable reuse but require build keys and lifecycle rules everywhere |
| Native backend | C11 first | LLVM or QBE changes emission and toolchain work without removing runtime migration |
| Escape mechanism | Typed foreign calls into a small shim | Raw C fragments shorten some ports but hide effects, dependencies, and semantics |
| Bootstrap profile | Explicit operation inventory, one worker, memory storage | Full runtime parity first delays the first closed loop but avoids profile divergence |
| Memory model | Preserve arenas and snapshot ownership | A new collector combines runtime conversion with a separate semantic and performance project |
| Generated artifacts | Release C archives with provenance | Committed C simplifies source-only builds but increases review noise and drift checks |
| Opcode source | Declarative metadata plus explicit handler builders | A richer instruction DSL can remove repetition but needs another language design |
| Generality | Reusable native library, one real runtime consumer | A multi-backend framework increases scope before the first bootstrap |

The first practical experiment is stage A plus one slice of stage B.
It generates tag operations, checked integer addition, and one real string construction operation through the proposed relations and builders.
The string operation copies borrowed input into arena-owned storage and publishes an immutable value only after successful construction.
Its tests cover empty and Unicode input, invalid lengths, allocation failure, and release of the owning arena.
The shim supplies allocation primitives. Generated code owns construction, error handling, and arena policy.

The experiment has five acceptance conditions:

1. Generated C compiles and produces independently specified values and errors for all three operations.
2. Ownership tests exercise success, failure, and arena release under sanitizers.
3. Deliberate type and effect errors produce diagnostics tied to the responsible instructions and call paths.
4. Different fact insertion and symbol creation orders produce identical generated C and stable metadata.
5. Reviewers can trace allocation, construction, errors, and release in the Mica descriptions without reading generated C to infer the algorithm.

The experiment records generation time, peak memory, source size, and C compilation time outside source control.
Its review selects whether to continue, revise the builders, or stop.
It does not expand automatically into a VM or kernel rewrite.
